clu.title: Bridging Syntax and Semantics: Distilling LLMs into Symbolic Rules for Few-Shot Relation Extraction
clu.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can recognize relations from a few labeled examples, but their limitations (i.e., violations of data privacy, security, regulatory requirements) can limit their deployment. We introduce a simple approach to few-shot relation extraction that distills an LLM's knowledge into reusable, editable symbolic rules, requiring no task-specific model training or LLM calls to classify new sentences. During offline preparation, an off-theshelf LLM paraphrases the labeled examples, and a syntactic parser extracts rules from the syntactic paths connecting the entities. At inference time, a symbolic multi-pass sieve matches parsed queries against these rules, progressively relaxing syntactic constraints to emphasize semantic cues while filtering weak matches. We evaluate on FS-TACRED and FS-FewRel. On 1-shot FS-TACRED, our method outperforms almost all neural and neuro-symbolic baselines in our comparison and comes within 0.31 F1 points of augmented Qwen3-4B classification, using approximately 22 times fewer neural parameters at inference time. With Llama 3.1-8B, our method outperforms direct LLM classification by 21.1 F1 points on 5-shot FS-TACRED. Further, across both datasets, our approach is less sensitive to LLM choice and reasoning settings than direct classification.

triage.title: Accuracy Is Not Safety: Ordinal, Calibrated Multimodal Prediction of KTAS Triage Levels
triage.abstract: Triage systems are central to emergency care, where rapid prioritisation must balance patient safety against resource constraints. The Korean Triage and Acuity Scale (KTAS) is a five-level ordinal scale whose application varies between nurses and errs towards under-triage. Prior KTAS models were flat classifiers evaluated by single-split accuracy, leaving their safety on the rare resuscitation level unknown. We present a multimodal model that predicts the KTAS level from the chief complaint, vital signs and demographics recorded at triage. A compact biomedical Transformer encodes the complaint, each modality is projected to a common scale before fusion, and a hybrid cross-entropy and Earth Mover’s Distance loss penalises errors by ordinal distance. On an expert-labelled cohort of 1,267 encounters under 5 × 10 repeated cross-validation, accuracy was 0.71 and Quadratic Weighted Kappa 0.73 (95% CI 0.70 to 0.77). Errors were 86% adjacent-level and split evenly between under- and over-triage, whereas 70% of nurse errors on the same cohort were under-triage; as a second reader it flagged 88 of 131 nurse under-triage cases. High-acuity calibration error was 0.015, and deferring the least confident half of encounters raised accuracy to 0.84. Twelve training objectives with accuracy between 0.68 and 0.71 identified between 0 and 18 of the 26 resuscitation cases; class weighting protected the critical class and ordinal shaping raised its recall further, so accuracy alone does not measure triage safety. Retrained on MIMIC-IV-ED, the approach identified critical encounters with a recall of 0.723 (95% CI 0.709 to 0.737), demonstrating severe-case identification with a precise performance estimate in a substantially larger cohort.

xmedfusion.title: XMedFusion: A Knowledge-Guided Multimodal Perception and Reasoning Framework for Autonomous Medical Systems
xmedfusion.abstract: Autonomous medical and robotic systems increasingly rely on intelligent perception and reasoning capabilities to interpret visual data and support clinical decision making. Radiology report generation represents a critical component of such automated diagnostic workflows, yet existing end-to-end multimodal models often suffer from weak visual grounding, resulting in unreliable interpretations and omission of subtle clinical findings. This paper presents XMedFusion, a modular AI framework designed as an intelligent perception and reasoning module for autonomous medical systems. The proposed framework decomposes visual information into coordinated functional components that emulate expert-driven analysis, including a visual perception agent that extracts image-grounded evidence, a knowledge graph construction agent that structures clinically relevant findings, and a retrieval-guided drafting process that ensures a consistent reporting structure. A synthesis agent iteratively integrates visual and structured evidence through reasoning-driven verification to produce reliable and interpretable diagnostic outputs. Experimental evaluation on a public chest radiograph dataset demonstrates significant improvements over baseline vision-language models, achieving gains from 0.0493 to 0.3359 in BLEU-1, 0.0863 to 0.2440 in ROUGE-L, and 0.0829 to 0.1708 in METEOR, along with substantial improvements in semantic evaluation metrics such as Consistency (2.38 to 7.80) and Accuracy (2.34 to 6.93). The results highlight the effectiveness of structured multi-agent perception and reasoning for enhancing robustness, transparency, and automation in intelligent medical imaging systems, enabling integration into autonomous healthcare and robotic diagnostic workflows.
